content:
Many definitions in mathematics concern special kinds of subsets of an algebraic object. For instance, a normal subgroup, or an intermediate field. These are defined in Mathlib in one of two ways:

  1. As a predicate on a simpler subobject: for instance, docs#Subgroup.Normal
  2. As a type of structures in its own right: for instance, docs#IntermediateField

Let's call approach (1) "unbundled", and approach (2) "bundled".

While upstreaming the theory of ring orderings from my real closed field project, I realised that my initial, bundled, formalisation of ring preorderings was wrong, and that they need to be unbundled instead. However, I have struggled to justify this design decision in subsequent unbundling PRs #37298 and #36863.

I'm proposing the following guideline:

Substructures should be bundled when they form a lattice under inclusion. Otherwise, they should be unbundled as predicates on the "most complicated" bundled subobject they are a special case of.

The reasoning is that I ran into issues with the bundled design precisely when I tried to define operations on ring preorderings, the collection of which which doesn't admit finite joins.

Does anyone have opinions on this? And how should this guideline be documented in Mathlib going forward?

(cc @Yaël Dillies )
Can you give more details on the claims that the bundled formalization was "wrong" and that ring orderings "need" to be unbundled?

Fair question! The full discussion is in the comments of #32077 (whose diff unfortunately changed to obscure the problem), but I'll give a summary. (I've explained some of this on Zulip before but it's best all in one thread).

Let RRR be a ring. A preordering P⊆RP\subseteq RP⊆R is a subset closed under +++ and ×\times× containing all squares and not containing −1-1−1. Preorderings are incredibly niche, and are only really used in a Zorny argument about the existence of orderings, which are subsemirings O⊆RO\subseteq RO⊆R generating RRR as a ring where O∩−OO\cap-OO∩−O is a prime ideal. Ring orderings are useful in real algebra because they correspond to quotients of RRR which are ordered domains, and so have an ordered fraction field.

The intersection of two preorderings is a preordering, but there is not necessarily such a thing as a preordering-closure -- that is, the poset of preorderings usually fails to have joins. This makes it hard to define operations like sSup, map and so on, which is what eventually killed the above PR. But some sort of supremum is necessary for the Zorn argument, and certainly you want to push forward orderings onto the quotient domain.

Of course, one can just define partial operations with junk values. That is what my original design did. However, I now think the better approach is to instead define preorderings as a predicate on Subsemiring, which does form a lattice under inclusion. My partial operations then become theorems about when the usual subsemiring operations preserve the "is a preordering" or "is an ordering" property. This produces an API that is easier to use downstream.

This philosophy then extends to other bundled subobjects that don't have joins for essentially the same reason: docs#AddGroupCone and docs#RingCone. I already PR'd the unbundled version of these structures: docs#AddSubmonoid.IsPointed.

Artie Khovanov said:

The intersection of two preorderings is a preordering, but there is not necessarily such a thing as a preordering-closure -- that is, the poset of preorderings usually fails to have meets.

I think you have join and meet backwards - the meet is the infimum, and the join is the supremum
yep sorry fixed

So what I think you're saying is: you have a predicate on subsemirings of a ring and the question is whether to make a type out of it. You're observing that the type would not have finite joins but that every chain has an upper bound, and want to draw conclusions about whether the type should exist or not from this. But in my mind a far more telling comment is your claim that this predicate is not really used at all except in one proof, which for me is stronger evidence that it should just be a predicate, with a proof that if every element of a chain of subsemirings satisfies the predicate then so does the sup.
I also think that the predicate approach is better. Note that docs#IntermediateField is different as one wants to write the Galois correspondence, so it's better to have a type.

@Kevin Buzzard well, the structure RingPreordering has already been PRed to Mathlib, so the question is whether to remove it. I do agree about minimising the usage of the resulting predicate given that it's only needed for this Zorn argument, and that that by itself is a good enough justification for unbundling.

I suppose I'm looking for a more general rule because the same question then comes up for (ring) orderings (currently docs#RingPreprdering.IsOrdering) and (group/ring) cones (currently docs#AddGroupCone and docs#RingCone; alternatively docs#AddSubmonoid.IsPointed), which all see mathematical applications beyond just one proof, and which could all plausibly be bundled. My claim is that these should all be unbundled.

@Riccardo Brasca That is true - there are special applications of the poset of intermediate field extensions, which provides a reason to bundle docs#IntermediateField. However, there are no such special applications for the poset of, say, subsemirings or submodules, yet they are bundled - I think rightly - as docs#Subsemiring and docs#Submodule. I think we can make the weaker justification that we have nice operations on that poset making it into a lattice - essentially, that we can take subsemiring and submodule closures of sets.

Yeah I suppose the difference is between like - so I think the normal subgroups form a lattice (indeed I think they famously form a modular lattice, though I've no idea where that exists in Mathlib and in what form), but that lattice I think has the same joins and meets. So that's somewhere where the unbundled form (Subgroup.Normal) makes sense.
Artie, do preorderings form a docs#ConditionallyCompletePartialOrderSup ?

@Wrenna Robson oh right yep sorry. That's interesting - same finite joins and meets, but different infinite ones (ie a different closure operator).

For what it's worth, the operations I want to define on preorderings and orderings are the same as the operations on the underlying subsemiring.

This raises the question of whether we should always unbundle subobjects if the operations we want on them are just the operations on some bigger subobject lattice. Probably not, right? I can't think of an example of the top of my head though.

I think so? But I haven't checked in Lean, and I remember running into problems with this last time I tried. Will look into it.
If the key application is Zorn then I would hope that it's even complete rather than just conditionally complete

Wikipedia lists several possible meanings of "complete partial order". For preorderings, nonempty directed sets have a supremum (because a directed union of preorderings is a preordering), but the empty set might not have a supremum. A ring has a preordering iff it is semireal; that is, if -1 is not a sum of squares. In this case, the least preordering is the collection of sums of squares.

This is all clear if you view a preordering as "a subsemiring containing the subsemiring of sums of squares, which doesn't contain -1." All you actually need to track in the inductive step of the Zorn argument is "doesn't contain -1."

So that's somewhere where the unbundled form (Subgroup.Normal) makes sense.

Interestingly, we have bundled docs#OpenNormalSubgroup (which I think is used in infinite Galois theory), but not bundled normal subgroup.
